title: Resetting a forgotten password
summary: Request a reset link from the sign-in screen; it stays valid for 30 minutes.
body: If you no longer have your credentials, choose "Can't get in?" on the sign-in screen and we will email a reset link to the address on the account. The link works once and expires after 30 minutes. Changing the password ends every other active session.

title: Magic links expire after 15 minutes
summary: Passwordless sign-in links are single use and short lived by design.
body: A passwordless link is bound to the browser that requested it and dies 15 minutes after it is issued. Opening it in a different browser, or after an email client has prefetched it, invalidates the link and you will be asked for a fresh one.

title: Two-factor codes are rejected
summary: TOTP codes depend on the clock of the device that generates them.
body: A time-based code is derived from the current time, so an authenticator on a device whose clock has drifted more than 30 seconds will produce codes the server refuses. Enable automatic time synchronisation on the phone and try again before falling back to a recovery code.

title: Saving and using recovery codes
summary: Ten single-use codes, shown once, that get you past two-factor when the phone is gone.
body: Recovery codes are generated when two-factor is switched on and are displayed exactly once. Each code works a single time. If you have used most of them, regenerate the set from Security settings, which immediately voids the old ones.

title: Changing the email address on your account
summary: The new address must be confirmed before the old one stops working.
body: Enter the new address under Profile and we send a confirmation to it. Until that confirmation is opened, notifications and reset links continue to go to the previous address. Addresses already used by another account are refused.

title: Ending every active session
summary: Sign out everywhere from Security settings when a device is lost or stolen.
body: Security settings list every session with its approximate location, browser and last activity. "End all other sessions" revokes the rest immediately, including mobile and desktop clients, which will ask for credentials on their next request.

title: Choosing a language and time zone
summary: Locale is per person, not per workspace, and exports always use UTC.
body: Interface language and time zone are stored on your own profile, so two people in the same workspace can see different formatting. Timestamps inside exports and API responses are always UTC regardless of what you pick here.

title: Your display name and avatar
summary: What other people in the workspace see next to your edits and comments.
body: Display name and avatar are shared across every workspace you belong to. An administrator who has enabled directory sync may overwrite both from the identity provider, in which case the fields are read only.

title: How long a session lasts before it ends by itself
summary: Idle timeout defaults to 30 days and can be shortened by an administrator.
body: By default a session survives 30 days of inactivity. Administrators on a business plan can lower the idle timeout, and any change applies to sessions that already exist, so people may be asked to authenticate again shortly after the policy is saved.

title: Using a passkey instead of a password
summary: Register the device you already unlock with a fingerprint or face.
body: A passkey replaces both the password and the second factor with the biometric your device already uses. Register one per device from Security settings. Passkeys are bound to the domain, which is what makes them resistant to phishing.

title: "Account temporarily locked" after repeated failures
summary: Ten consecutive bad attempts trigger a fifteen-minute cooldown.
body: The lock is automatic and clears itself after fifteen minutes; nobody has to unlock it for you. If it keeps happening, an old client or a saved credential somewhere is likely retrying a stale password in the background.

title: Merging two accounts created with different addresses
summary: Support can move content, but the accounts themselves cannot be combined.
body: Two separate registrations remain two identities. What support can do is transfer authored documents and workspace memberships from one to the other, after which the emptied account can be deleted. Comment attribution is rewritten; version history is not.

title: Closing your personal account
summary: Deleting an identity is separate from deleting a workspace.
body: Closing your account removes your profile and personal settings and releases the email address for reuse. Documents you created inside a shared workspace stay there and are reattributed to a deactivated user. Transfer ownership first if you are the only owner of a workspace.

title: Why we ask you to verify a new location
summary: A sign-in from an unfamiliar network triggers an emailed confirmation.
body: When the network, device fingerprint and rough geography all look new at once, we email a six-digit confirmation before letting the session start. Travelling and corporate VPN exits are the two most common innocent causes.

title: Signing in with Google or Microsoft
summary: Social identity is matched to your account by verified email address.
body: The first time you use a provider we match the verified address it returns against an existing account and link the two. If your workspace enforces SAML, the provider buttons are hidden and only the corporate identity provider is offered.

title: Contrast, motion and text size settings
summary: Accessibility preferences that follow you across devices.
body: Increase contrast, reduce animation and scale interface text from Accessibility settings. Reduced motion also respects the operating system setting automatically, so you rarely need to set it twice.

title: Payment authorization failures
summary: A refusal comes from the issuing bank, not from us.
body: When a charge is refused, the decision was made by the bank that issued the card. The three usual causes are insufficient funds, an expired card, and a regional block on foreign or online merchants. The bank rarely tells us which, so calling them is faster than retrying.

title: Updating the card on file
summary: A workspace holds one default instrument; replacing it does not retry old invoices.
body: Billing settings keep a single default payment method. Replacing it takes effect on the next cycle and does not immediately re-attempt invoices that already failed — those follow the normal retry schedule, or you can settle one by hand from the invoice itself.

title: Invoices and VAT receipts
summary: Every charge produces a downloadable PDF under Billing → History.
body: Each successful charge generates a PDF invoice showing the amount, the period and any tax applied. Add your company details and tax identifier before the charge is raised: documents already issued cannot be reissued with new details.

title: Adding a tax identifier to your billing profile
summary: A validated VAT or GST number removes tax from future charges where the rules allow.
body: Enter the identifier in Billing → Company details and we validate it against the relevant registry. Reverse charge is applied from the next invoice onward for business customers in eligible jurisdictions; earlier invoices stand as issued.

title: Switching from monthly to annual
summary: The unused part of the current month becomes credit against the annual charge.
body: Moving to an annual term takes effect immediately. We credit whatever remains of the paid month and charge the difference, so the amount you see at checkout is already net of that credit. Moving back to monthly is only possible at renewal.

title: How proration works when you change plan mid-cycle
summary: Upgrades are charged at once and downgrades take effect at renewal.
body: An upgrade produces an immediate charge for the remainder of the period, calculated by the day. A downgrade is queued for renewal rather than refunded, so you keep the higher tier for the time already paid for.

title: How seats are counted and charged
summary: Billing starts when an invitation is accepted, not when it is sent.
body: A seat is consumed by any member or admin who has accepted an invitation. Guests with access to a single document are free and never consume one. Removing somebody frees the seat at the next renewal rather than producing an instant refund.

title: What happens when an invoice cannot be collected
summary: Four attempts over ten days, then the workspace moves to read only.
body: We retry a failed invoice on days one, three, six and ten. Administrators are emailed after every attempt. If the tenth attempt fails the workspace becomes read only: nothing is deleted, and paying the outstanding invoice restores write access within a minute.

title: Refunds and credit notes
summary: Refunds go back to the original instrument; credits offset the next invoice.
body: A refund is returned to the card or account that paid and typically appears within five working days. Where a refund is not possible we issue a credit note instead, which is drawn down automatically against future invoices until it is exhausted.

title: Paying by bank transfer against a purchase order
summary: Available on annual plans above a threshold, arranged with the sales team.
body: Annual contracts can be invoiced for payment by transfer on 30-day terms, with your purchase order number printed on the document. Card details are not required in that arrangement, and the workspace is not affected by the automatic retry schedule.

title: Cancelling a subscription
summary: Cancellation stops renewal; it does not end the period you have paid for.
body: Cancelling from Billing leaves the plan fully active until the end of the current term, after which the workspace drops to the free tier. You can undo a cancellation at any point before that date without contacting anybody.

title: What the free tier keeps after a paid plan ends
summary: Documents stay readable; the features above the free limits are locked, not deleted.
body: Everything you created remains and stays readable. Content over the free limits — extra members, version history beyond 30 days, saved searches — is locked rather than removed, and resubscribing restores access to all of it untouched.

title: Currency and regional pricing
summary: The currency is fixed at first purchase and follows the billing country.
body: We charge in the currency matching the billing country you first entered. Changing it later requires cancelling and resubscribing, because an active subscription cannot switch currency mid-term.

title: Discounts, coupons and nonprofit pricing
summary: One coupon per subscription, applied before tax.
body: A coupon entered at checkout applies to the subscription line before tax and cannot be combined with another. Registered nonprofits and accredited educational institutions can apply for a standing discount by sending proof of status to billing support.

title: Spending alerts and usage caps
summary: Get warned before metered usage turns into a surprise on the invoice.
body: Set a soft threshold that emails administrators when metered usage crosses it, and optionally a hard cap that refuses further metered calls for the rest of the period. Caps apply to API and storage overage only; seats are never capped.

title: Reading the usage breakdown on your invoice
summary: Each metered line shows quantity, included allowance and the overage rate.
body: Below the subscription line, every metered dimension appears with the quantity consumed, what the plan includes and the unit price for the excess. The daily detail behind any line can be downloaded as CSV from the invoice page.

title: Inviting teammates to a workspace
summary: Invitations are emailed, expire in seven days, and consume a seat once accepted.
body: Invite people by address from Members, optionally choosing their role up front. An unopened invitation expires after seven days and can be resent. Nothing is billed until somebody accepts.

title: What each role can do
summary: Owner, admin, member and guest, from most to least privileged.
body: Owners control billing and can hand over the workspace. Admins manage people and settings but cannot delete the workspace. Members create and edit content. Guests reach only the specific documents shared with them and never see the member list.

title: Transferring workspace ownership
summary: Only the current owner can hand over, and only to an existing admin.
body: Pick a successor from Members → Ownership; they must already be an administrator and must accept within 48 hours. The previous owner keeps administrator rights afterwards unless somebody removes them, which is the step people most often forget when a colleague leaves the company.

title: Removing somebody and reassigning their work
summary: Choose whether their private documents are transferred or archived.
body: When you remove a member, anything they authored in shared spaces stays where it is. Their private documents must either be transferred to a named person or archived; if you skip the choice, the default is to archive, and an administrator can still recover them later.

title: Guest access for people outside your company
summary: Guests see only what is shared with them and never consume a seat.
body: Invite an external collaborator to a single document or folder and they become a guest. Guests cannot browse the workspace, see other members or use search beyond what they have been given. Administrators can list every guest and their reach from Members → Guests.

title: Running more than one workspace
summary: One identity can belong to many workspaces, each billed separately.
body: Workspaces are isolated from one another: separate members, separate content and separate invoices. The switcher in the sidebar moves between them without signing out. Content cannot be linked across a workspace boundary.

title: Combining two workspaces into one
summary: There is no merge button; the practical route is an export and import.
body: Workspaces cannot be merged in place. Export the smaller one, import it into the larger as a folder, then invite its members and close the original. Version history does not survive the round trip, so keep the source workspace read only for a while rather than deleting it straight away.

title: Deleting a workspace and the 30-day window
summary: Deletion is queued for 30 days and is reversible until it completes.
body: An owner can queue deletion, which immediately makes the workspace inaccessible while keeping the data recoverable for 30 days. Any owner can cancel during that window. Once it elapses the content is destroyed and no export can be produced afterwards.

title: Groups: changing permissions for many people at once
summary: Grant access to a group and manage its membership in one place.
body: A group is a named set of people that can be used anywhere an individual can. Sharing a folder with the group means new joiners inherit access the moment they are added. Groups can be synced from your identity provider rather than maintained by hand.

title: Letting people join automatically by email domain
summary: Anybody with a verified company address can join without an invitation.
body: Verify ownership of a domain by publishing a DNS record, then choose whether matching addresses join automatically or simply request access. Domain capture applies only to new registrations; existing accounts on that domain are listed so you can claim them deliberately.

title: Renaming a workspace and changing its address
summary: The slug in the URL can be changed once every 30 days.
body: Renaming is cosmetic and takes effect at once. Changing the slug rewrites every workspace URL: old links redirect for 30 days and then stop working, so tell people before you do it and update anything hard-coded in integrations.

title: Seeing exactly who can reach a document
summary: The access panel resolves every direct, inherited and group-derived grant.
body: Open Share → Who has access to see a flattened list of everybody who can reach the document, with the reason next to each name: shared directly, inherited from a parent folder, or via a group. Administrators see the same panel for any document in the workspace.

title: The workspace activity log
summary: Administrative and content events, retained for a year on business plans.
body: The log records sign-ins, permission changes, deletions, exports and integration installs, each with the actor, the time and the source address. Entries cannot be edited or removed by anybody, including owners, and can be streamed to your SIEM.

title: Posting an announcement to everybody
summary: A banner shown to every member until they dismiss it.
body: Administrators can publish a short notice that appears above the sidebar for all members, optionally with an expiry date. Announcements are not emailed; use them for things people should see next time they are working, not for anything urgent.

title: Restoring something you removed by mistake
summary: Removed documents sit in Trash for 30 days before they are destroyed.
body: Open Trash in the sidebar, find the item and choose Restore; it returns to its original location with its history intact. After 30 days the entry is purged, and only an administrator with a point-in-time restore can help.

title: Version history and reverting
summary: Every save is a version; restoring one adds a new version rather than erasing any.
body: History groups edits into sessions and keeps them for 30 days on free plans and indefinitely on business plans. Restoring an earlier state appends it as the newest version, so the intervening work is never lost and can itself be restored.

title: When two people edit the same paragraph
summary: Concurrent edits are merged automatically; only true conflicts are surfaced.
body: Edits are merged character by character, so simultaneous work in different parts of a document simply combines. A conflict marker appears only when the same span is rewritten by two people while one of them was offline, and both versions are kept side by side for you to choose.

title: Working without a connection
summary: Recently opened documents stay editable offline and sync when you return.
body: Anything you opened in the last week is cached locally and remains editable with no network. Changes queue on the device and replay in order once the connection returns. A document that was never opened on that device cannot be reached offline.

title: Comments, mentions and resolving threads
summary: Mentioning somebody notifies them and grants read access if they lacked it.
body: Select text and comment to start a thread. Typing @ and a name notifies that person, and if they could not previously open the document you are asked whether to share it with them. Resolved threads are hidden but never deleted.

title: Suggesting changes instead of making them
summary: Suggestion mode records edits as proposals for somebody else to accept.
body: Switch the mode selector from Editing to Suggesting and your changes appear as tracked proposals rather than taking effect. Anyone with edit rights can accept or reject them individually or in bulk. Reviewers are limited to suggesting whether they choose the mode or not.

title: Importing from Word, Markdown and Google Docs
summary: Structure and basic formatting survive; complex layout does not.
body: Headings, lists, tables, links and images are converted faithfully. Multi-column layouts, text boxes, footnotes and revision marks are dropped or flattened. Import a copy first and check the result before retiring the original.

title: Exporting a document to PDF
summary: Page size, margins and whether comments are included are all configurable.
body: Export from the document menu and choose page size, orientation and margins. Comments can be appended as endnotes or omitted. Very long documents are rendered on the server and emailed as a link rather than downloaded in the browser.

title: Templates and reusable blocks
summary: Promote any document to a template, or save a fragment for reuse.
body: Templates live in a workspace gallery and can carry placeholder fields that are filled in when somebody starts from them. A reusable block is smaller: a saved fragment that keeps a link back to the original, so updating it can propagate everywhere it is used.

title: Embedding files, images and video
summary: Drop a file in to attach it, or paste a link to embed a live preview.
body: Images and short video are stored with the document and served from our CDN. Pasting a link to a supported service embeds a live preview instead of a copy, which means the embed follows the source if it is later changed or removed.

title: Upload size limits
summary: 50 MB per file on free plans and 5 GB on business plans.
body: The per-file ceiling is 50 MB for free workspaces and 5 GB for paid ones; total workspace storage is a separate quota shown in Billing → Usage. Uploads that exceed the ceiling fail immediately rather than partway through.

title: Tables: sorting, formulas and column types
summary: Typed columns unlock sorting, filtering and simple arithmetic.
body: Give a column a type — text, number, date, select or person — and the table gains sorting and filtering for it. Formula columns support arithmetic and a small set of functions over other columns in the same row, recalculated as you type.

title: Linking documents and finding what points here
summary: Every inbound link is listed at the foot of the target document.
body: Type @ followed by a title to link to another document. The target collects a backlink automatically, which is what the Referenced by section at the bottom lists. Backlinks respect permissions: you never see a reference from a document you cannot open.

title: Locking a document against further edits
summary: Freeze the content while leaving it readable and commentable.
body: Locking prevents edits by everyone including the author, which is useful once something has been approved. Comments remain open unless you close those too. Any administrator, and the person who locked it, can unlock it again.

title: Duplicating a document
summary: A copy carries the content and structure but starts a fresh history.
body: Duplicating produces an independent document with none of the original's version history, comments or sharing. If you need the history to travel with it, move the original and create the copy in its place instead.

title: Keyboard shortcuts
summary: Press ? anywhere to see the full list for your platform.
body: The palette on Ctrl+K, or Cmd+K on a Mac, reaches any command by name and is usually faster than remembering an individual chord. Shortcuts can be remapped under Preferences → Keyboard for anybody used to a different editor.

title: Search results look out of date
summary: The index is updated incrementally and can trail an edit by about a minute.
body: Edits are queued for indexing rather than applied synchronously, so a document changed seconds ago may still be described by its previous contents. A minute is typical; anything beyond five minutes is worth reporting.

title: How results are ranked
summary: Text relevance, recency and your own activity, in that order of weight.
body: Ranking starts from term relevance, with matches in the title weighted more heavily than matches in the body. Recently edited documents and documents you have opened before are then boosted. Nothing about the ordering is configurable today.

title: Search operators
summary: Quote a phrase, prefix a term with a minus, or filter by author and date.
body: Double quotes require an exact phrase and a leading minus excludes a term. The filters author:, in: and before:/after: narrow by person, folder and date, and can be combined freely with ordinary words.

title: Searching inside PDFs and attachments
summary: Text-bearing attachments are extracted and indexed; scans need OCR.
body: PDFs, Word files and plain text attachments have their contents extracted at upload and become searchable alongside the document that holds them. A scanned page with no text layer is only found by its filename unless OCR is enabled for the workspace.

title: Keeping a document out of search
summary: Exclude an individual document or a whole folder from indexing.
body: The Exclude from search switch in document settings removes an item from everybody's results while leaving it reachable by direct link. Applying it to a folder covers everything inside, including items added later.

title: Saved searches and alerts
summary: Store a query and optionally be emailed when new documents match it.
body: Save any query, filters included, to rerun it from the sidebar. Turning on an alert emails you at most once a day with documents that have started matching since the last message. Alerts are personal and never reveal anything you cannot already open.

title: Searching across several workspaces at once
summary: Not supported: each workspace has its own isolated index.
body: A query only ever runs against the workspace you are currently in, because indexes are isolated for tenancy reasons. The desktop client's quick switcher can search titles across every workspace you belong to, which covers most of what people want here.

title: A document you can open does not appear in results
summary: Usually exclusion, a stale index, or a permission grant that arrived recently.
body: Check the exclusion switch first, then wait a minute in case the document was just edited. If access was granted to you within the last few minutes the index may not yet reflect it, since permission changes are applied to search asynchronously.

title: Rebuilding the workspace index
summary: An administrator can force a full reindex; it runs in the background for hours.
body: A full rebuild is available under Settings → Search and is rarely necessary. While it runs, results come from the old index and are progressively replaced. Large workspaces take several hours and there is no way to pause it once started.

title: Searching in languages other than English
summary: Stemming and stop words follow the workspace language setting.
body: Word normalisation is language specific, so the workspace language decides how terms are reduced before matching. Documents in a language other than the workspace default are still found, but only by exact word forms rather than by their stems.

title: Webhook deliveries are failing
summary: Six attempts with exponential backoff, then the endpoint is disabled.
body: A delivery that does not receive a 2xx within ten seconds is retried six times over roughly a day. Consistent 4xx responses disable the endpoint and email the owner; it stays disabled until somebody re-enables it, which also replays the queue.

title: Verifying the X-Atlas-Signature header
summary: Every delivery is signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw request body.
body: The X-Atlas-Signature header carries a timestamp and a hex digest. Recompute the HMAC over the exact bytes you received — not a re-serialised object — using the endpoint secret, and compare in constant time. Reject anything with a timestamp older than five minutes.

title: The webhook retry and backoff schedule
summary: Delays double from 30 seconds up to six hours across six attempts.
body: Retries are spaced 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, 45 minutes, 3 hours and 6 hours after the original attempt. Every retry carries the same event identifier, so consumers must be idempotent rather than assuming exactly-once delivery.

title: Choosing which events an endpoint receives
summary: Subscribe to specific event types rather than everything.
body: An endpoint subscribes to a list of event types, optionally narrowed to one folder. Subscribing to everything is discouraged: high-volume events such as document.updated will dominate your queue and slow delivery of the ones you care about.

title: Setting up the Slack integration
summary: Link a channel to a folder and choose which events are posted.
body: Install from the directory, authorise the Slack workspace, then map each folder you care about to a channel. Unfurling of Atlas links respects permissions: somebody who cannot open a document sees only its title in the preview.

title: Connecting GitHub repositories
summary: Reference issues and pull requests, and keep their status in sync.
body: Authorise the GitHub App against the organisations you want. Pasting an issue or pull request link renders a live status chip that updates when the item is closed or merged. The integration reads metadata only and never has access to source code.

title: Attaching files from Google Drive and OneDrive
summary: Pick a file to embed a live reference rather than copying it.
body: The picker embeds a reference that resolves against the source each time it is viewed, so permissions stay with the original service. Readers who lack access there see a placeholder telling them whom to ask.

title: Automating with Zapier and Make
summary: Prebuilt triggers and actions for people who would rather not write code.
body: Both platforms expose our common events as triggers and our create and update calls as actions, authorised with an ordinary API token. They poll on their own schedule, typically every few minutes, so they are not a substitute for webhooks when latency matters.

title: Calendar sync is creating duplicate entries
summary: Almost always two connections writing to the same calendar.
body: Duplicates appear when the same calendar is connected from two workspaces, or when both the personal and the workspace-level connection are active. Disconnect one of them; existing duplicates are not cleaned up automatically and have to be removed by hand.

title: Disconnecting an integration cleanly
summary: Revoke on both sides, or the third party keeps a valid token.
body: Removing an integration here revokes our token for it, but an app that also holds an OAuth grant in your account should be revoked there as well. Content the integration created stays in place and is not removed with it.

title: Rotating an integration secret without downtime
summary: Two secrets can be valid at once during a rotation window.
body: Generating a new endpoint secret keeps the previous one working for 24 hours, during which deliveries are signed with both. Deploy the consumer that accepts either, then retire the old secret manually rather than waiting for it to lapse.

title: Building a private integration for your own workspace
summary: A private app skips review and is only installable where it was created.
body: Create it under Settings → Developer to get a token scoped to that workspace alone. Private apps are not listed publicly and are not reviewed by us, which makes them the right choice for internal automation. Publishing later requires a separate submission.

title: Which addresses our webhooks come from
summary: A published, stable set of egress addresses you can allowlist.
body: Outbound deliveries leave from a fixed list of addresses published at the well-known endpoint and changed with at least 30 days' notice. Allowlisting them is the usual way to accept deliveries at an endpoint that is otherwise closed to the internet.

title: Sandbox workspaces for testing
summary: A free, disposable workspace with the full API and no billing.
body: Every paid plan includes one sandbox that behaves identically to production, points at the same API surface under a separate host, and is wiped on request. Data cannot be moved between a sandbox and a real workspace.

title: Generating and revoking API tokens
summary: The value is shown once at creation and cannot be recovered afterwards.
body: Create a token under Settings → Developer, copy it immediately and store it in a secret manager. Revocation is instantaneous and irreversible: in-flight requests using it fail with 401 rather than being allowed to finish.

title: Rate limits on the public API
summary: 600 requests per minute per token; exceeding it returns HTTP 429.
body: The limit is applied per token in a sliding one-minute window. A rejected request returns 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds — honour it rather than retrying immediately, since tight retry loops extend the window instead of shortening it.

title: Paginating with cursors
summary: Follow the opaque next_cursor rather than computing offsets.
body: List endpoints return at most 100 items with a next_cursor when more exist. Cursors are opaque and stable across inserts, which offset-based paging is not; treat them as strings and never try to construct one yourself.

title: The bulk import endpoint
summary: Up to 1,000 documents per call, processed as one asynchronous job.
body: POST the batch to /v3/documents:import and you receive a job identifier straight away. The job is atomic per document, not per batch, so a malformed entry fails alone and is reported in the job result rather than aborting the rest.

title: Idempotency keys
summary: Send the same key to make a retried write safe.
body: Any write accepts an Idempotency-Key header. A repeat within 24 hours returns the original response instead of acting twice, which is what makes a client-side retry after a timeout safe. Keys are scoped to the token that used them.

title: Reading an API error response
summary: Errors follow RFC 9457 problem+json with a stable type URI.
body: Every failure returns application/problem+json carrying type, title, status and detail, plus a request identifier. Branch on the type URI rather than the human-readable title, which we reserve the right to reword at any time.

title: API versioning and how deprecation works
summary: The major version is in the path and supported for 18 months after replacement.
body: Breaking changes only ever arrive in a new major version. When one is superseded, the Sunset header appears on every response to the old version and we email token owners at 180, 90 and 30 days. Additive changes ship to the current version without notice.

title: The OAuth authorization flow
summary: Authorization code with PKCE; implicit grant is not supported.
body: Redirect to /oauth/authorize with a code challenge, exchange the returned code at /oauth/token, and refresh with the rotating refresh token you receive. Access tokens last an hour, refresh tokens 30 days, and a refresh token is invalidated the moment it is used.

title: Scopes and least-privilege tokens
summary: Grant the narrowest scope that works; scopes cannot be widened later.
body: Scopes are granular per resource and per verb, such as documents:read or members:write. A token's scopes are fixed at creation: broadening them means issuing a new token, which is deliberate. Requests outside the granted set fail with 403 rather than 401.

title: Installing and authenticating atlas-cli
summary: Available through Homebrew, npm and a static binary.
body: Install with brew install atlas-cli, npm i -g atlas-cli, or by downloading the release binary. Running atlas-cli auth login opens a browser for the OAuth flow and stores the token in the system keychain rather than in a dotfile.

title: Polling a long-running job
summary: Poll the job resource, or subscribe to the completion event instead.
body: Imports, exports and reindex operations return a job identifier. Poll /v3/jobs/{id} no more often than every two seconds, or subscribe to the job.completed webhook and skip polling altogether. Job records are kept for seven days.

title: Timestamps and date formats in the API
summary: RFC 3339 in UTC everywhere, with no local time anywhere.
body: Every timestamp we emit is RFC 3339 with a trailing Z, and we accept the same on input. An offset other than Z is converted rather than rejected. Date-only fields have no time component and are never shifted by a time zone.

title: Requesting only the fields you need
summary: A fields parameter trims the response and the work behind it.
body: Pass fields=id,title,updated_at to receive just those properties. Omitting the body of large documents is the single most effective way to speed up a listing call, since the content is fetched from a different store than the metadata.

title: Testing against the sandbox API
summary: A separate host, separate tokens, and no rate limits worth worrying about.
body: The sandbox answers on api.sandbox.atlas.example with tokens that are not valid in production and vice versa. Rate limits are ten times higher and webhook deliveries are also sent, which makes it the right place to exercise a consumer end to end.

title: Official SDKs and supported runtimes
summary: TypeScript, Python, Go and Ruby, generated from the OpenAPI description.
body: The four official clients are generated from the same OpenAPI document that backs the reference, so they gain new endpoints on the day those ship. Retries, pagination and idempotency are handled for you. Community clients exist for other languages and are not supported by us.

title: Subscribing to live updates over a websocket
summary: A persistent connection for changes you would otherwise poll for.
body: Open a socket to /v3/stream, authenticate with a short-lived ticket rather than your token, and subscribe to the documents or folders you care about. The connection is dropped after an hour and clients are expected to reconnect with backoff.

title: Reducing background activity on mobile
summary: Background refresh keeps the cache warm and is the main cost when the device is idle.
body: Periodic wakeups exist so that opening the app is instant. On a device where power matters more than that, turn off background refresh under Settings → Sync; content then updates when you open the app instead. Push notifications continue to arrive either way.

title: Push notifications never arrive
summary: Check the operating system permission before anything else.
body: A permission that was declined once is not asked for again and has to be granted in system settings. Beyond that, low power mode suppresses delivery on some devices, and notification rules set in your profile apply to mobile as well as email.

title: Downloading documents for offline reading
summary: Pin a folder to keep it on the device regardless of the cache policy.
body: Anything you open is cached for a week, but a pinned folder is downloaded in full and kept until you unpin it. Pinning a large folder over a mobile connection is deferred until the device is on Wi-Fi unless you override it.

title: The app is taking up a lot of storage
summary: Cached documents and attachments account for nearly all of it.
body: Settings → Storage shows the split between pinned content, cache and application data, and clears the cache on request. Clearing removes nothing from the server and nothing you have pinned; it only forces the next open to fetch again.

title: Unlocking with Face ID or a fingerprint
summary: A local lock on top of the session, not a replacement for it.
body: Biometric unlock protects the app on a shared or lost device and can be set to trigger immediately or after a delay. It is checked locally: it does not re-authenticate you against the server, and it does not extend a session that has already ended.

title: Sending things to Atlas from other apps
summary: The share sheet captures links, text and images into a chosen folder.
body: Atlas registers as a share target, so anything shareable can be captured without switching apps. Pick a default destination in Settings → Capture to skip the folder prompt every time. Captures made offline are queued and uploaded later.

title: The app closes immediately on opening
summary: Almost always a corrupt local cache after an interrupted upgrade.
body: Reinstalling clears the local store and fixes it in nearly every case; nothing that has finished syncing is lost. If a crash happens on a device that has never worked, send us the identifier from the store page rather than reinstalling repeatedly.

title: Tablet layout and split view
summary: Two panes on a large screen, with the divider remembered per device.
body: On a tablet the list and the document share the screen, and the app supports the system split-view alongside another application. Attaching a keyboard enables the same shortcuts as the desktop client.

title: Limiting sync to Wi-Fi
summary: Keep large transfers off a metered connection.
body: Settings → Sync can restrict attachment downloads and pinned-folder refreshes to Wi-Fi while leaving text sync always on, since text is negligible. Roaming is treated as metered even when the connection reports otherwise.

title: Home screen widgets and quick capture
summary: Jump straight into a new note or a pinned document.
body: The small widget opens quick capture in one tap; the larger one lists recently opened documents. Widgets refresh on the system's schedule, which can lag by a few minutes and is not something an application can control.

title: Which operating system versions are supported
summary: The current release and the two before it, on both platforms.
body: We support the current major release of each mobile platform and the two preceding it. Older devices keep the last compatible build from the store and continue to work, but stop receiving features and eventually security fixes.

title: Joining the mobile beta
summary: Public betas run through TestFlight and the Play beta channel.
body: Seats are limited and refreshed monthly. Beta builds can contain unfinished features and are not covered by support commitments; report problems through the in-app shake gesture, which attaches the relevant logs automatically.

title: The desktop client is using a lot of memory
summary: Decoded previews dominate; lowering preview quality releases most of it.
body: The renderer keeps decoded images and document previews in memory so that scrolling stays smooth. On a machine under pressure, set preview quality to Low under Preferences → Performance and clear the local cache, which together typically halve the footprint.

title: Everything is slow after moving to version 3
summary: A one-time local store migration runs on first launch.
body: Version 3 rewrites the local store into a new format the first time it starts. On a large workspace that takes several minutes, during which the client is deliberately throttled. It runs once per device; if slowness outlives the migration, collect diagnostics and send them to us.

title: Automatic updates and release channels
summary: Stable by default, with beta available and both controllable by policy.
body: The client checks for an update hourly and applies it on the next restart. Administrators distributing the app centrally can pin a version or disable self-updating entirely through the managed policy file.

title: Installing without administrator rights
summary: A per-user installer that writes only inside your own profile.
body: The per-user package installs into the profile directory and needs no elevation, at the cost of not registering the protocol handler system-wide. Deployment at scale should use the machine-wide MSI or PKG with your management tooling instead.

title: Installation fails with error 0x80070005
summary: An access-denied code from the installer, usually caused by policy or antivirus.
body: The code means access denied. In practice it is either a group policy forbidding installation into the target directory, or endpoint protection holding a lock on it. Retry with the per-user installer, and if that also fails send us the installer log from the temp directory.

title: Running the client behind a proxy
summary: System proxy settings are honoured; PAC files and NTLM need configuration.
body: The client follows the operating system proxy by default. A PAC script is supported, and an explicit proxy can be set in the managed policy. Proxies requiring NTLM need the credentials in the policy file, because the client will not prompt for them.

title: A global shortcut is being taken by another app
summary: Remap ours, since we deliberately never steal a registered shortcut.
body: Global shortcuts are registered at startup and one that is already taken silently fails rather than overriding the other application. Choose a different combination in Preferences → Keyboard, or quit the app holding it and restart the client.

title: Using two accounts at the same time
summary: Profiles keep separate sessions, caches and windows.
body: Add a profile from the account menu to run a second identity in parallel; each has its own window, cache and notification settings. Switching between profiles does not sign either of them out.

title: Clearing the local cache
summary: Safe at any time, provided nothing is still waiting to sync.
body: Preferences → Performance → Clear cache removes downloaded content and forces a fresh fetch. Check the sync indicator first: clearing while changes are queued discards them, and the client warns you but the warning is easy to dismiss.

title: Collecting diagnostic logs for support
summary: Help → Collect diagnostics produces a redacted archive.
body: The archive contains client logs, versions and timings. Document contents are excluded and identifiers are redacted before the file is written, so it is safe to attach to a ticket. Verbose logging can be enabled first if we ask for it.

title: Flickering, blank panes and other rendering glitches
summary: Nearly always graphics acceleration on an old driver.
body: Turn off hardware acceleration under Preferences → Performance and restart. If that fixes it, updating the graphics driver usually lets you turn it back on. Remote desktop sessions should leave acceleration off permanently.

title: Removing the client completely
summary: Uninstalling leaves the cache and preferences behind unless you say otherwise.
body: The uninstaller offers to remove local data as well; declining keeps your cache and preferences so that reinstalling restores the previous state. Nothing stored on the server is affected either way.

title: ERR_TLS_HANDSHAKE on a corporate network
summary: An intercepting proxy is presenting a certificate the client does not trust.
body: Inspection appliances terminate TLS and re-sign traffic with an internal authority. The client trusts the system store, so add the corporate root there, or exempt our API hostname from interception. Certificate pinning is not used, so a correctly installed root is enough.

title: Configuring SAML single sign-on
summary: Supply the identity provider metadata and map the email assertion.
body: Paste the metadata URL, map the email attribute, and decide whether just-in-time provisioning may create accounts on first sign-in. Test with one account before enforcing SSO for everybody, because a misconfigured mapping locks out the whole workspace at once.

title: Rotating the SAML signing certificate
summary: Two certificates can be trusted at once so rotation causes no outage.
body: Add the new certificate before the old one expires and both are accepted until you remove the old entry. We email administrators 30 and 7 days before a configured certificate lapses; an expired one presents as a generic authentication failure for every user simultaneously.

title: SCIM provisioning and deprovisioning
summary: Create, update and deactivate accounts from your directory automatically.
body: The SCIM 2.0 endpoint accepts user and group operations from any conformant provider. Deactivating somebody in the directory ends their sessions here within a minute and frees the seat at renewal. Group pushes map onto workspace groups one to one.

title: Allowing only managed devices
summary: Device posture rules reject sessions from hardware you do not control.
body: When device trust is enforced, a session is only issued to a client presenting a certificate from your management platform. Enrolment is handled entirely by your MDM; we verify the certificate and nothing else. Guests are exempt unless you include them explicitly.

title: Restricting access by network address
summary: Allowlist the ranges your people work from, with a break-glass exception.
body: An address allowlist rejects sessions originating anywhere else, including the API unless you exempt tokens. Always configure a break-glass account excluded from the rule: without one, a change to your egress addresses locks every administrator out at the same time.

title: How your content is encrypted
summary: TLS 1.3 in transit and AES-256 at rest, with keys rotated quarterly.
body: Traffic uses TLS 1.3, with 1.2 still accepted for older clients. Stored content and backups are encrypted with AES-256 under keys held in a managed HSM and rotated every quarter. Customer-managed keys are available on the enterprise plan.

title: Where your data is stored
summary: Choose a region when the workspace is created; it cannot be changed later.
body: Content is held in the region picked at creation and does not leave it, apart from a small amount of account metadata used for routing. Moving an existing workspace to another region means exporting and recreating it.

title: Sub-processors, SOC 2 and other reports
summary: Current reports are available in the trust centre under NDA.
body: The sub-processor list is published and changes are announced 30 days ahead for anybody subscribed to the notification. SOC 2 Type II and penetration test summaries are downloadable from the trust centre once an NDA is in place.

title: Reporting a vulnerability
summary: Send it to the security address; we acknowledge within one working day.
body: Report findings to security@atlas.example with enough detail to reproduce. Testing against your own workspace is welcome; testing against another customer's is not. We do not currently pay bounties but we do credit reporters who ask to be named.

title: Alerts for unusual sign-in activity
summary: Administrators are notified about impossible travel and credential stuffing.
body: We flag sign-ins that could not physically follow the previous one, and bursts of failures across many accounts at once. Alerts arrive by email and in the activity log, and can be forwarded to a webhook for your own tooling to act on.

title: Requiring two-factor for everybody
summary: Enforce it workspace-wide with a grace period for people who have not enrolled.
body: Turning on enforcement gives unenrolled members a configurable grace period, after which they must enrol before doing anything else. Accounts that authenticate through SAML are exempt, since the identity provider is responsible for the second factor there.

title: Placing a workspace under legal hold
summary: Suspends deletion so that nothing can be destroyed while the hold stands.
body: A hold overrides retention policies and the Trash purge, keeping everything recoverable including items members believe they have deleted. Holds are visible in the activity log and can only be lifted by an owner.

title: Running your own penetration test
summary: Allowed against your workspace with notice, under the published rules.
body: Tell us the window and source addresses at least five working days ahead so our own defences do not treat it as an attack. Denial-of-service testing and social engineering of our staff are excluded. A summary of findings is appreciated but not required.

title: Requesting a full export
summary: Everything as JSON plus the original files, delivered as a download link.
body: Start an export from Settings → Data and we email a link when it is ready, typically within an hour. The link expires after seven days. Only administrators can export a whole workspace; anybody can export a single document they can open.

title: What is inside an export archive
summary: Documents, comments, members and files — but not version history.
body: The archive holds one JSON file per document with its comments and metadata, a manifest, a member list, and the uploaded files under their original names. Version history and activity logs are deliberately excluded because of their size.

title: Importing an export into another workspace
summary: Supported, but links between documents are rewritten and history is lost.
body: Upload the archive under Settings → Data → Import. Internal links are remapped to the new identifiers, and anything pointing outside the archive becomes plain text. Member references are matched by email address where an account exists.

title: Erasing someone's personal information on request
summary: A subject erasure request is completed within 30 days.
body: Submit the request from the privacy console with the address concerned. We remove profile data and attribution, replacing authorship with a deactivated placeholder, and confirm in writing. Content the person wrote inside shared documents is not deleted, since it belongs to the workspace.

title: Anonymising an account that has left
summary: Keeps the work and severs the identity behind it.
body: Anonymising replaces the name, address and avatar with an opaque placeholder everywhere they appear, including comments and version history. It cannot be undone and does not release the seat, which you remove separately.

title: Automatic deletion after a retention period
summary: Rules can purge documents in a folder once they reach a chosen age.
body: Define a policy per folder in days since last edit. Matching documents move to Trash and follow the normal 30-day purge from there, so the effective lifetime is the policy plus thirty days. Legal holds suspend every policy while they are in force.

title: Backups and point-in-time restore
summary: Continuous backup with a 35-day window, restored by our team on request.
body: Backups run continuously and allow a workspace to be returned to any moment in the last 35 days. Restores are performed by us, take several hours, and replace the entire workspace rather than individual documents. Use Trash and version history for anything smaller.

title: Producing a copy for a customer's legal team
summary: A scoped export limited to named documents, with a chain-of-custody manifest.
body: Administrators can export a selection rather than the whole workspace, producing a manifest with a checksum per file and the time of extraction. That manifest is what makes the bundle usable as evidence, so keep it with the archive.

title: What ends up in our logs
summary: Request metadata for 30 days; never document content.
body: Operational logs record addresses, timestamps, endpoints and identifiers, kept for 30 days and then discarded. Document contents are never written to a log. Support staff reach content only through an audited break-glass process that notifies workspace owners.

title: Cookies and product analytics
summary: Essential cookies always; analytics only where you have opted in.
body: Session and security cookies cannot be disabled because sign-in depends on them. Product analytics are off by default in regions that require consent, and an administrator can switch them off for an entire workspace regardless of individual choices.
